brief_summary: Do/don't diagram split into two panels. Left panel, marked with a coral check, shows a switch puller's jaws hooked symmetrically under the switch housing lip pulling straight upward with even arrows on both sides, captioned 'legs exit the socket straight — contact arms stay true.' Right panel, marked with a warm-red X, shows a screwdriver levering one side of a tilted switch housing at an angle against the socket, with a bent/splayed contact arm called out, captioned 'side-load bends the receptacle — next switch seats loose.'
data_sources: hot-swap-sockets-tradeoffs.mdx § 'What the socket costs, physically' — 'Pulling a switch out at an angle, or levering it out against the housing edge with a fingernail or a flathead screwdriver instead of using a proper puller, puts side-load on the legs and can bend the socket's spring contact — sometimes badly enough that the socket stops gripping the next switch reliably.'

hot-swap-sockets-tradeoffs.mdx § 'What the socket costs, physically' — 'seat a switch puller's jaws under the switch housing, not the stem, and pull straight up with even pressure. No rocking, no prying at an angle... A switch puller is built to apply vertical force evenly across both sides of the housing at once; fingers and screwdrivers are not.'
